primary_reviews.support: Verses 1–6 move from the confession that the Lord has been Israel's dwelling through divine eternity to the human return to dust, then linger on sleep and morning grass as images of transience. primary_reviews.counterevidence: Ps.90.1–17 remains the necessary parent poem, but as the only retrievable unit it would flatten the change from contemplation of creaturely brevity to confession of wrath and then to direct pleas for compassion. The grass image reaches its evening end in 90:6; the first explicit we are consumed in your anger belongs to the next movement.

primary_reviews.support: The opening plea to be heard unfolds as an emaciation lament: days vanish like smoke, bones burn, appetite fails, the speaker is isolated like desert birds, and ashes and tears become his food. His life finally stretches and withers like a shadow at 102:11; But you, Yahweh, will remain forever at 102:12 reverses the focus from wasting petitioner to enduring God.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Ps.102.1–28 is the complete prayer and must remain the parent, but as the sole unit it conceals the poem's sharp my days / but you remain contrast. The restoration of Zion and creator permanence answer the lament; they are not part of the lament's first-person wasting catalogue.

The corporate Zion hymn has already reached its terminus at 102:22.

primary_reviews.support: Ps.104.1–9 praises the creator's cosmic architecture—light as clothing, heavens as tent, cloud chariot, winds as messengers, earth founded, waters fleeing and assigned a boundary. The prohibition that the waters not cover the earth again completes cosmic ordering; verse 10 narrows from bounded ocean to springs coursing through valleys and habitats.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Ps.104.1–35 remains the encompassing creation hymn, but it cannot replace a locator for the primordial ordering scene. Later verses describe provision, time, creature dependence, and praise; they presuppose rather than continue the specific earth-and-waters ordering completed at 104:9.

The catalogue of supplied habitats ends with wild goats and rock badgers; 104:19 turns from place and food to moon, sun, seasons, and daily time.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Ps.104.1–18 would couple cosmic ordering with the habitats it enables, a valid larger sequence, but it erases the 9/10 change from restraining waters to distributing them for life. The shorter unit follows a single provisioning logic from spring to mountain refuge.

primary_reviews.support: The moon's appointed seasons and the sun's setting introduce a compact alternation: darkness releases forest animals and lions, sunrise gathers them to dens, and the human worker then goes out until evening. Once the day's human labor closes at 104:23, the exclamation Yahweh, how many are your works! starts a new inventory of manifold creatures.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Ps.104.19–30 unites temporal ordering with the creatures who live under it, but it merges a day-night vignette with the sea-and-dependence meditation. The 104:24 exclamation restarts the praise and expands its subject beyond the rhythmic alternation of 19–23.

primary_reviews.support: Yahweh, how many are your works! at 104:24 opens a panoramic creature inventory, moving to the sea, ships and Leviathan, then to all creatures waiting for food. Giving and hiding, gathering breath and death, sending Spirit and renewed creation carry the movement to its natural completion in 104:30.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Ps.104.19–30 would present time and creature dependence together, but the new exclamation at 24 and the sea-wide expansion make a real rhetorical restart. Moon/sun scheduling in 19–23 is a finished vignette; 24–30 asks how the multitude exists moment by moment from divine provision and breath.

primary_reviews.counterevidence: The whole Ps.104.1–35 is the primary hymn, yet whole-only retrieval makes the shift from describing creation to voicing wishes and vows invisible. Verses 31–35 look back over every preceding work rather than adding another created domain to the catalogue.

primary_reviews.support: Verse 6 opens with the purpose that the beloved be delivered, followed by plea and divine speech over Shechem, Succoth, Gilead, tribal emblems, and neighboring peoples. Questions about entry into Edom, acknowledgment of divine rejection, and the closing appeal for help carry one military-rescue movement through 108:13.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Ps.108.1–13 best preserves the final Psalm and may rightly be the primary retrieval object. Still, merging 6–13 into an undifferentiated whole obscures the shift from universal praise to a petition framed by oracle and battlefield questions. Child exposure is acceptable only if it never substitutes for the parent.

A child at 1–5 can mark the accusation report without deciding whether 6–20 is the petitioner's imprecation or adversarial speech being reported. If metadata cannot preserve that ambiguity and hydrate the parent, keep the Psalm whole.

primary_reviews.counterevidence: Ps.119.33–48 combines He's petitions with Waw's anticipated answer and is rhetorically attractive. It should remain a paired-stanza reading, but it crosses the source-attested He/Waw boundary at 41 and changes from repeated divine imperatives to the arrival of loving kindness and a speaker's promised witness.

primary_reviews.counterevidence: The complete Ps.137.1–9 is essential, especially because lament, oath, and imprecation belong to one exilic poem. Yet whole-only retrieval suppresses the concrete riverside scene and its closing impossibility question before the speaker changes rhetorical mode.

primary_reviews.support: Verses 5–6 form a two-part self-curse: if the speaker forgets Jerusalem, let the right hand lose skill; if Jerusalem is not remembered and exalted above joy, let the tongue cling to the palate. Verse 7 redirects remembrance outward into judgment against Edom.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Ps.137.1–6 unites the setting with the vow it provokes, but it crosses from communal narration and captor demand into first-person oath. The two-verse unit is not arbitrary: matched conditional curses on hand and tongue enact the threatened loss of playing and singing.

primary_reviews.support: The remembrance appeal at 137:7 begins the final judgment request against Edom for urging Jerusalem's destruction; Babylon is then addressed as doomed, and two severe beatitudes imagine retaliation. These wishes run without another reset to the Psalm's end.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Ps.137.1–9 prevents the imprecation from being detached from displacement, coercion, and the Jerusalem oath and must be mandatory parent context. The whole, however, should not hide the explicit transition from self-directed remembrance in 5–6 to an appeal concerning Edom and Babylon in 7–9.

primary_reviews.support: The paired questions Where could I go…Where could I flee? open a survey of heaven, Sheol, dawn's wings, the far sea, and darkness; every imagined destination remains reached and guided by God. Verse 12 concludes that darkness and light are alike to him, while 139:13 begins a causal explanation from bodily formation in the womb.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Ps.139.1–12 joins omniscience and inescapable presence and is a valid larger theological movement. It nevertheless crosses the 6/7 rhetorical restart: the first section states what God knows, whereas 7–12 tests whether any location or darkness can escape that knowing presence.

primary_reviews.support: From 144:12 the focus becomes communal flourishing: mature sons, sculpted daughters, full storehouses, multiplying flocks, strong cattle, unbreached security, and quiet streets. Two beatitudes close the Psalm by calling such a people happy and finally identifying as happy the people whose God is Yahweh.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The complete Ps.144.1–15 carries the needed chain from warrior dependence and rescue to communal well-being. A 12–15 child can expose the flourishing tableau, but it must not imply that prosperity is detached from the prayer or that the debated Then at 12 is certainly a new independent start.

primary_reviews.support: Ps.145.1–7 begins with the king's daily resolve to exalt and bless, then moves generation by generation through unsearchable greatness, mighty works, glorious majesty, awesome acts, abundant goodness, and sung righteousness. Verse 8 introduces the established gracious-and-merciful formula, changing from proclamation of deeds to a character-and-kingship meditation.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: The undivided Ps.145.1–21 best protects the received, imperfectly transmitted alphabetic praise and its universal close. Universal goodness prompts works and saints to praise his kingdom's glory and power through the confession of everlasting dominion at 13; verse 14 turns to those who fall and are bowed down.
primary_reviews.counterevidence: Ps.145.1–13 forms a broad greatness-and-kingship hymn and may be preferable if the gracious formula is read as the climax of verses 1–7 rather than a restart.
